svg.text: HashLife above a memo floor, the rule as a bit-sliced circuit below it
Every picture and number is drawn from the measurement harness. The components were measured separately: GHL has not yet run as one program.
the universe: a grid of tile IDs
hit path: one probe per tile
the grid s/2 generations on; repeat
miss path: waves, one per level
at the floor: an atlas of windows
real patterns; colour is the cell state

Curves: the share of tile-steps not yet in the memo table, for tiles of 16×16 cells (Life: 32×32), against the generations run so far (log scale; the ROM's curve is that of a smaller ROM of the same kind, 1,548 × 1,461 cells, the soup's that of
a 512 × 512 soup). The figure is the share over the second half of the run. This novelty, not density, decides the engine: the ROM is new for one period and then entirely known, the soup stays new.
Below the floor: the rule as a circuit
Hutton32b, 32 states, as two-input gates on bit-planes
32 cells of squares (marked in panel 3) and their four neighbours
Checked while drawing: on all 357,120 cells of
this frame the network gives the next generation
of the pattern's own rule table, Hutton32.
entries. Mismatches on all of them: 0.
Every gate works on a 32-bit word, one bit per cell. Wire shade: on how many of the 32 cells the signal is 1 (light: none, dark: all). A signal with several consumers is one wire with branches.
Life-like rules (B/S notation) need one plane. A carry-save adder tree counts the live neighbours of 32 cells in 26
operations; the rule's birth and survival sets are decoded from the four count bits.
Brute force, measured, in cell-updates per second
Above the floor: tiles, IDs and a memo table
the hit path: a gather of four IDs and one probe per tile
hit path built on the GPU
squares at generation 20,480, cut into 16×16-cell tiles. One sweep advances 8 generations with one probe per tile: 1,472
probes, 651 distinct keys, 103 results not in the table (7.0 %, marked). Novelty sits where the circuit is computing; everything
else is a hit. The white frame is taken apart on the right.
A tile's ID is its slot in the tile
equal IDs and a universe is a
grid of IDs: 4 bytes per tile.
Above the tiles every key is
four IDs. Only IDs are hashed,
A memo entry: four IDs give one ID
the key: the four IDs framed above
A 32×32 window and the 16×16 tile in its centre 8 generations later. This entry was missing in this
sweep. Checked while drawing: the circuit of panel 2, applied 8 times, gives the same tile.
The memo table, slot by slot
The first 3,840 of 1,048,576 slots (32 MiB) after 65,536 generations: open addressing, linear
probing, 1.49 probes per insert. 1.17·107 probes found 520,613 distinct windows; the floor windows
under them took 3.3 % of the cell-updates delivered. The rest were hits.
A miss: the recursion in waves, level by level
One wave per level, each a batch for one dispatch
A missed window asks for nine windows half its size, then for four more: two waves a level
down. Each box is a wave; its number is the windows that missed, its dark part their share of
squares, the 64 generations from 20,480: mostly known
a ROM, its first 64 generations: all new
35 and 36 waves brute-force 2,918 and 573,210 floor windows. A wave is 16 dispatches of
fixed capacity: 50 µs measured for an empty one.
At the floor: an atlas of missed windows
35 of the 203 windows of one floor wave of squares.
Each missed 16×16 window is copied from its four 8×8 base tiles into a grid of
bit-planes, the circuit of panel 2 steps the grid 4 generations, and the centre of
every window (outlined) is interned as a base tile. The stages of a wave (claim,
expand, evaluate, intern, publish) are each one dispatch over the whole batch.
Above the floor a miss costs probes and inserts only.
Per universe, dispatch latency picks the depth
A generation costs its dispatches (from 3.2 µs each) however small the universe,
so few active cells cannot pay for a deep recursion. The model's thresholds for
plain cells, memo only above: 42 regions
256×256-cell regions, by the mode they spent most
of the first 1,024 generations in. Content that is new
at every scale (the ROM while it is being learned,
part of a movie) is stepped as cells; the rest keeps
its memo. Model time 18.6 ms; plain cells
Why a floor, and what it buys
Measured rates put the memo floor
A probe costs as much as ρ = RB / RP cell-updates of brute force. The probe rate is the same
for every rule; the brute-force rate is not. Rates per second:
What a hit saves, V / ρ: a w×w window gives its centre w/4 generations later, V = w3/16
1×: a hit saves what a probe costs
A window is worth a memo entry only if its result is worth more than the probe that finds it:
from 16×16 windows on for the 32-state rule (3.2×; 8×8 windows: 0.40×) and from 32×32 for
Life (5.4×; 16×16: 0.67×). That is each rule's memo floor: a larger ρ puts it one level coarser.
Golly memoizes down to 4×4 blocks, worth V = 4.
Against Golly 5.1 at its best step size: rate of the GHL component that ran, over Golly's
the same with the CPU's learning time counted
the recursion on one CPU thread
Golly leads where content recurs sparsely and runs are long; there GHL falls back to the recursion. Every GPU result was checked against the
CPU, and the CPU engine's final states equal Golly's.
